data.title: Bill that could change the nickel, how you pay with cash passes through House
data.description:
(NEXSTAR) – A new penny, bound for circulation, hasn’t been minted in nearly a year. Yet the U.S. is still working to get rid of it, once and for all.

A step in that process happened Monday in the House of Representatives, where the latest version of the Common Cents Act passed by voice vote. An identical version of the bill passed in the Senate with unanimous consent last month.

The bill passed Monday varies slightly from another version of the Common Cents Act that made its way through the House and to the Senate earlier this year. While that version instructs the Treasury to stop minting the penny, it did not explicitly outline the discontinuation of a coin.

The formal end of the penny may be the chief aspect of the bill, but the Common Cents Act could also impact how you pay with cash and potentially pave the way for the U.S. to get a new nickel. Here’s what to know.

The death of the penny, sort of

The U.S. Mint stopped producing pennies last year, but it has released collectible pennies for America’s 250th anniversary.

The Common Cents Act, if enacted, wouldn’t change either of those practices. The penny would be formally sent to the bench, though one-cent coins “for sale as numismatic items” can still be produced.

As they do now, pennies would remain legal tender. The bill that most recently passed the House notes that “any one-cent coin that is minted and issued on any date before the date of the enactment of this subsection shall remain legal tender for all debts, public charges, taxes, and dues.”

It’s estimated that more than 300 billion pennies are out in the world — more than 800 pennies, or $8 worth, per U.S. citizen — trapped wherever a little Lincoln can hide.

Pay with cash? You may see change

If you’ve paid with cash within the last year or so, you may have found that retailers do not have any pennies to give you, despite how many are believed to be rolling around in the world.

Though the Common Cents Act would not help those pennies (perhaps lost in couches and collecting dust in piggy banks) get back into circulation, it would address some of the difficulties of paying with cash that have materialized.

Businesses would be allowed the option to round cash transactions to the nearest nickel. That would make a $1.82 purchase a $1.80, while $1.83 would become $1.85, for example. As simple as it sounds, some states and localities have laws prohibiting the practice. Advocates believe the Common Cents Act could iron out that confusion.

An overhaul of the nickel

With the penny handled, the Common Cents Act would also focus on the nation’s second-lowest denomination: the nickel.

The five-cent coin may have some added value as of late, especially among retailers who have had to round change on cash transactions. But it still remains extremely expensive to produce. It cost 13.31 cents to produce a single nickel in fiscal year 2025, down slightly from 13.78 cents in fiscal year 2024. Last year marked 20 consecutive years that nickel production costs remained above the coin’s face value.

One expert has even argued it would have been easier for the U.S. to ditch its nickel than the penny.

The Common Cents Act would not get rid of the nickel, but it could lead to a change in its composition. The bill allows the Treasury Secretary to test and evaluate compositions of the coin and suggest a new make-up for the nickel if it “reduces the cost” of production and “has a minimal adverse impact on machines designed to accept coins.”

That may include making the nickel out of zinc, with an outer layer of nickel. Only the penny and the $1 coin currently use zinc, which was nearly $7,000 per tonne cheaper than copper last year, the Mint reports.

Changing a coin’s composition can be difficult, though. Attempts to make the penny cheaper, for example, failed.

No changes to the nickel or how you pay with cash can take effect until the bill becomes law. And before you rush out to stock up on nickels, it’s worth noting that, according to at least one expert, that hoarding pennies may have contributed to their death. A bill that would cease the production of the nickel was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services last summer.

data.title: Republicans kept their promise: America's border is secure again
data.description:
For four years under the Biden administration, Americans watched our southern border collapse. Record numbers of illegal crossings poured into the country. Cartels flourished. Fentanyl flooded our communities. Criminal illegal immigrants, including members of the violent Tren de Aragua gang, embedded themselves in my home state of Colorado and across the United States.

The previous administration’s open-border policies were a choice. That chaos ended when President Trump returned to office and Republicans in Congress kept the promise we made to the American people.

At the start of the 119th Congress, I voted for the Laken Riley Act, which requires the detention of illegal immigrants charged with theft, burglary or similar crimes. Named after the young woman murdered by an illegal immigrant who should never have been free to walk our streets, this law is a straightforward step to protect American communities from preventable violence.

Since January 2025, the results have been dramatic and undeniable. Daily encounters at the southwest border have plummeted by roughly 95 percent, falling from more than 5,000 per day under the Biden administration to about 250. For months at a time — now more than a year straight — zero illegal immigrants have been released into the U.S. Apprehensions are at historic lows, including the lowest fiscal-year Border Patrol total since 1970. Deterrence is working again because the policies changed.

A secure border also protects American health care. Cartel fentanyl, emergency-room costs, and benefit fraud drain hospitals and taxpayers. Stopping that at the border keeps care available for veterans, seniors, and families who play by the rules. I authored the Fentanyl is a WMD Act to treat cartel poison as a mass-casualty threat; I passed a bipartisan House amendment requiring the Department of Homeland Security to report how many illegal aliens are deported for assaulting law enforcement; and I introduced legislation to stop federal health insurance dollars from covering people here illegally.

When fentanyl, fraud, and uncompensated emergency care flood rural hospitals, nurses and families on the Eastern Plains pay the price. A secure border stops that poison before it reaches our neighborhoods. It ends the deadly trek that cartels sell to migrants, and it removes criminals who never should have been here.

That is not a slogan. It is the difference between families whose loved ones come home at night and those who never do.

Securing the border does more than keep Americans safer. It also slashes the fraud and waste that exploded when millions of illegal immigrants were funneled into public systems. When the border is closed and interior enforcement is real, taxpayer dollars stop being siphoned off by illegal claims, emergency costs and benefit abuse. That money can go where it belongs: to American citizens who actually need it — veterans, seniors, working families, schools, and health care for people who play by the rules.

Republicans did what they promised: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, set aside $46.5 billion for border barriers and technology. Steel is going in the ground for primary and secondary walls, Rio Grande water barriers, sensors, and roads are going up from California to Texas. Dozens of miles are finished; hundreds more are under construction.

When Democrats once again shut down the government and attempted to defund Customs and Border Protection and ICE — and reopen the border — I voted for the Secure America Act. This legislation provides multi-year mandatory funding for Border Patrol and ICE through the end of Trump’s term, delivering roughly $70 billion to hire, train, equip, and retain the agents and officers who enforce our laws. It strengthens interior enforcement, expands detention capacity, supports removals, and ensures these critical agencies are fully funded without being held hostage by the defund the police crowd during annual appropriations deliberations.

I support expansion of the 287(g) program, which lets federal and local police identify and remove criminal illegal immigrants. More cooperation is needed to protect communities from violent offenders and drug traffickers who entered under the previous administration’s policies.

Some will never admit it, but a secure border works. Crime is down, fewer gang members are on the streets, and states like Colorado can put more money into education and health care for American citizens instead of cleaning up open-border chaos. Ignore the socialist propaganda and paid protests. More than a year of zero releases proves we are safer. Voters demanded an end to catch-and-release and the removal of criminal aliens. Republicans delivered. America is safer, and American tax dollars are better protected.

Now Congress must finish the work by codifying Trump’s executive orders into statute. Future administrations should not be able to flip a switch and reopen the border. I will continue fighting to ensure these gains are permanent.

Lauren Boebert represents Colorado’s 4th District in Congress and serves on the House Committee on Natural Resources and the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform.

data.title: Durbin: Trump moves on voting 'most serious challenge' since Civil War
data.description:
Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) on Tuesday said President Trump’s policy proposals and executive orders on voting have created the “most serious challenge” to the U.S. government since the Civil War.

CNN’s Sara Sidner asked Durbin, the ranking member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, if Democrats have a “plan to secure voter rights.” Durbin replied that Democrats have attempted to bring up this issue “a number of times.”

“The right to vote is critical to citizenship, and this president is clearly on a mission to discourage people from voting and to not count all the votes that are cast,” Durbin continued. “I think this is the most serious challenge to our basic constitutional form of government since the Civil War. I think it‘s that serious. And yes, we‘re doing everything we can, but as a minority party, we need more votes.”

Sidner noted the Supreme Court’s block on Trump’s executive order to require states to upload lists of voters to receive mail ballots, as the president has long accused mail-in voting of being fraudulent, though there has been no evidence of such fraud at the massive scale that Trump has suggested.

She asked Durbin if Trump could attempt to restrict mail-in voting again leading into the 2028 presidential election.

“We are prepared for the likelihood that this president will do anything in his power to discourage people from voting, to not count the votes that are cast and to question the qualifications of voters at every level,” the Illinois Democrat said. “He is desperate because this is a referendum on his leadership and he is doing poorly with the American people.”

The high court, which previously ruled in Trump’s favor on the plan, ruled against the attempt to have the U.S. Postal Service implement new design requirements, including an official logo and barcode, on ballots before Election Day.

A whistleblower previously warned that the U.S. Postal Service’s computer system was riddled with errors that, if left untouched, would result in “a ‘catastrophic failure’ of the system that could ‘derail the midterm elections,'” according to a letter from Sen. Richard Blumenthal’s (D-Conn.) office.

Trump blasted the majority of the court that ruled against him, including Justices Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett, all Trump appointees who sided with the liberal minority. He accused his appointed justices of being “merely a shell of their original selves.”

The president has also urged GOP leaders in Congress to eliminate the Senate filibuster in order to pass the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, his legislative priority that would require Americans to prove their citizenship to register to vote and to show photo ID before casting their ballot.

Efforts to pass what Trump has called his legislative priority have so far failed, though some GOP lawmakers like House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) have suggested passing parts of the bill as part of a reconciliation package.

data.title: Pentagon acknowledges space weapons deployment for first time
data.description:
The United States has launched a weapon into orbit that will be used to protect American troops, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed Monday.

Speaking at the annual Air, Space and Cyber Conference at National Harbor, Md., Meink did not give details as to the type of weapon that is now in space or when it was launched, but said it will “make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”

“Today we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenges of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said. “This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”

Meink also said it is “critically important that we maintain our dominance not only in the air but in space.”

Citing a U.S. official, The Washington Post reported that the weapon could allow the military to take out an enemy’s satellite should it be used to target American troops or a U.S. satellite.

This is the first time a U.S. official has acknowledged the country has such a space capability after warning that China and Russia were developing their own weapons to threaten U.S. satellites and forces. 

The admission quickly roiled Beijing and Moscow, with the Chinese Foreign Ministry on Tuesday warning Washington to “stop preparing for war” in space.

“China stands for peaceful use of the outer space and keeping it safe, and opposes any arms race in outer space or any attempt to weaponize it and turn it into a warzone. We urge the U.S. to stop its military build-up in the outer space, and uphold global strategic stability with concrete actions,” the ministry posted to X.

The Kremlin also responded Tuesday, according to state media.

“We believe that space must be free of any weapon,” spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters in Moscow. “We are counting on broad international consolidation to continue working toward the complete demilitarization of space.” 

Meink on Monday brushed aside potential criticisms from the two countries, telling reporters: “Is there any question . . . about whether or not the Chinese or Russians have been developing these sorts of weapons?”

In addition to a space-based weapon, the Pentagon is currently developing the Golden Dome missile defense system, which will include interceptor layers and a space-based missile warning and tracking system. Golden Dome is projected to cost about $1.2 trillion to develop, deploy and operate over the next 20 years, according to the Congressional Budget Office.

data.title: AI's architects made a choice. Now they're calling it fate.
data.description:
Recently Dean Ball, formerly the chief architect of Trump’s artificial intelligence action plan, issued a mea culpa for downplaying the risks of AI technologies that he knew could go “very, very poorly for human beings.” His essay was prompted by revelations of AI’s rogue capabilities, demonstrated by an alarming incident this summer in which an experimental application within OpenAI executed an unauthorized cyberattack on a company called Hugging Face.

Woven throughout Ball’s apology is an assertion that the emergence of dangerous, “self-sovereign” AI agents was inevitable. “There is probably nothing we could have ever done to avoid this outcome under even the best of circumstances,” he writes. Currently head of strategic futures at OpenAI, Ball acknowledges a culture of profound mistrust among Americans regarding pervasive digital technologies. He does not explore its roots, but laments that an atmosphere of suspicion makes a “genuine loss of control event” with AI harder to preempt. 

Claims for inevitability regarding technological creations that pose existential threats have a long, colorful history. A close parallel with AI is nuclear weapons.  

The initial rationale for the atomic bomb’s creation was to defeat Nazi Germany to the nuclear finish line, akin to the supposed imperative for the U.S. to outcompete China in the AI race. Once it was clear that Germany posed no nuclear threat, other rationales surfaced to guarantee forward momentum on a project whose irresistible allure lent it an air of inevitability. As physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer explained, “When you see something that is technically sweet you go ahead and do it and you argue about what to do about it only after you have had your technical success.”

OpenAI’s Sam Altman has likened himself to Oppenheimer — and AI to the Manhattan Project — citing the physicist’s belief in the inevitability of scientific progress. “Technology happens because it is possible,” Altman explained in an interview. He even mused that he and Oppenheimer share a birthday, as if to suggest their rendezvous with destiny.  

Yet nothing in science or technology is destined to happen. The creation of potentially self-sovereign AI, like the drive to build atomic bombs, was a choice. 

Now that the “warning shot” has occurred — OpenAI’s term for the Hugging Face incident — what can be done? Can we learn from history? 

One suggestion, stemming from the extensive post-mortem conducted in the wake of this incident, is to create an independent agency akin to the National Transportation Safety Board, tasked with investigating plane crashes and making its findings available to the public. The parallel is imperfect: plane crashes are visible and widely documented. By contrast, the AI industry conducts itself in secrecy, ranging from nondisclosure agreements for data center creation to lack of transparency regarding data used to build models. Nevertheless, some such agency would be a start.

A second, more ambitious recommendation is an internationally agreed upon slowdown of AI development combined with minimal safety standards, a move called for by many in the AI industry. Given the U.S. economy’s dependence on the industry, this effort is likely to face resistance. But long-term benefits could greatly outweigh the risks. 

Precedents exist for halting forward motion on powerful technologies. In 1975, international biologists, lawyers and journalists gathered at Asilomar in California to hash out a genetic truce in light of hazards posed by recombinant DNA. Rather than ban genetic research, the agreement called for strict, risk-based safety guidelines. 

The research pause was brief but effective. As Nobel Laureate Paul Berg observed, Asilomar “marked the beginning of an exceptional era for science and for the public discussion of science policy.” To be sure, commercial and military interests were already lurking behind the scientific debate. Nevertheless, the conference allowed a contentious technology to flourish, with numerous public health benefits.

In 2017 an “Asilomar for AI” gathering was held on the grounds of the 1975 conference. There, a set of 23 guidelines was created, emphasizing “safe, ethical, and transparent AI” and shared prosperity. The principles stated that “development of advanced AI should be pursued only when its effects can be aligned with the long-term well-being of humanity.” 

Judging by recent events, many of those principles appear to have been abandoned. The industry has helped to foster the culture of mistrust its chief architects cite as an obstacle to preventing greater AI harms. It remains a legitimate question whether voluntary self-regulation is possible or sufficient. 

The European Union, meanwhile, has launched the AI Act, the first comprehensive and binding legal framework classifying AI systems by risk and setting obligations for how organizations develop, deploy, document and govern AI. 

Ball’s widely read essay is simultaneously an apology for complicity and a denial that culpability exists where a technology is simply bound to emerge. Yet legislation like the EU AI Act is proof that the future of AI — and any technology — is a matter of choice, not fate. We should act on that knowledge now. 

Lisa H. Sideris is a recent Public Voices fellow of the OpEd Project and a scholar of science, religion and environmental ethics at the University of California, Santa Barbara.

data.title: Pentagon tells Congress Iran war cost at least $42 billion
data.description:
The Pentagon told Congress last month that the cost of the war against Iran has now climbed over $42 billion, a $4.5 billion increase on the most recent public estimate from the Department of Defense more than six months into the conflict. 

Defense officials provided the updated cost estimate on Aug. 13 to congressional defense committees, a congressional aide told The Hill on Monday. The Pentagon did not respond to a request for comment on how much the cost has increased in the ensuing month. 

The figure marks the first official update from the administration on the war since July, when Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate during a hearing in July that the estimated cost of the conflict was $37.5 billion. 

Some experts The Hill spoke to in July placed the topline number far higher. 

Linda J. Bilmes, the Daniel Patrick Moynihan Senior Lecturer in Public Policy at the Harvard Kennedy School, said at the time the cost of the war was about $100 billion. 

Democrats in Congress have repeatedly asked the Pentagon and the Trump administration to provide the full cost of the conflict. 

Last week, the Pentagon’s comptroller’s office said on social platform X that the department — along with the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) — provided Congress more than 10 “timely updates” on the cost of the conflict, including information on “obligations, operational costs and unfunded replacement costs.” 

The comptroller’s office said Wednesday the latest update with the conflict’s cost estimate was sent on Aug. 28. When reached for comment on Thursday, the office, led by Jules “Jay” Hurst, referred The Hill back to the social media post. 

“The Department will continue to keep transparency and accountability with Congress as mandated by law, without compromising the security of our servicemembers,” Hurst’s office said in the post. 

The Hill has also reached out to Hegseth’s office and OMB for comment on the latest cost estimates. 

The House Armed Services Committee (HASC) has received weekly briefings for a “couple” of months regarding the war, but has not received the total cost of the conflict, another congressional source told The Hill on Monday. 

The Iran war has cost at least $1,200 per household, the left-leaning Center for American Progress estimated on Aug. 20.

The Trump administration’s push for additional funding from Congress remains at a standstill.  

In June, the White House requested over $87 billion for a supplemental package, with about $67 billion to replenish munitions used up during the Iran war and other military operational costs.

The GOP-controlled House passed a $95 billion package in July aimed at funding the Iran war and other White House priorities, but the deal has not made progress in the Senate, where Democrats have blocked its passage. 

President Trump requested a record-setting $1.5 trillion defense budget for fiscal 2027, arguing it is necessary to harden the military and protect national security. The administration has looked to pass $350 billion through the partisan process of reconciliation, but the window has largely closed for such a heavy lift before the midterms.

data.title: Live updates: Patel faces surprising questions in Senate; Bessent pressed on tariffs, $5K dividend
data.description:
FBI Director Kash Patel is testifying before the Senate Judiciary Committee for an oversight hearing on Tuesday morning.

Ahead of the meeting, Patel released a letter sent to panel chair Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) to explain expenditures that have drawn scrutiny. But questioning during the hearing turned to an unexpected topic: Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) grilled Patel as he tried “to understand” a recent change in policy regarding bestiality. The line of questioning was sparked by a shift in FBI hiring practices that lifted longtime bans on selecting new trainees if they have engaged in prostitution or bestiality.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent spent the morning in the House Financial Services hearing, facing questions on tariffs, artificial intelligence and more.

Earlier Tuesday, President Trump upbraided the Supreme Court for its 7-2 ruling against his mail-in ballot restrictions the evening prior.

“These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves, a Court that is costing the United States Trillions of Dollars with shockingly bad rulings that are of such magnitude that it won’t be easily possible for our Country to recover or heal,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Attorney General Todd Blanche will brief reporters in the Rose Garden on Tuesday, becoming the latest administration official to step in since the departure of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt.

Trump has an ambassador credentialing ceremony followed by policy meetings.

First lady Melania Trump is in Jefferson, N.C., for an event focused on rehabilitation after the devastation of 2024’s Tropical Storm Helene.

Follow along live below.

data.title: Russian businessman paid for Trump Jr. wedding after-party: Five things to know
data.description:
New reports of Russia-tied financial backing for the after-party events at the May wedding of President Trump’s eldest son have sparked concerns about potential influences from foreign adversaries in the U.S. government ahead of the midterm elections. 

Russian oligarch Umar Kremlev funded lavish wedding celebrations for Donald Trump Jr. and socialite Bettina Anderson in the Bahamas, including a private island and a fireworks show, according to a ProPublica investigation published on Monday. 

The report raised alarm from Democrats and national security experts about potential ethics violations, as the president and members of his family are typically expected to avoid accepting pricey gifts from adversaries like Russia. 

Here are five things to know about this unusual wedding gift:

Who is Umar Kremlev?

Kremlev is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a controversy-plagued sports organization financed by Russia’s state-owned natural gas company, Gazprom. 

The International Olympic Committee removed IBA from its role organizing boxing events at the global sporting event in 2023, citing the group’s refusal to provide transparent financial information. 

Kremlev appealed this decision to Trump in an open letter following his second inauguration last year, expressing the IBA’s interest in seeing the sport represented at the 2028 games in Los Angeles. 

“We are very interested in bringing this event back to your country, and we are more than ready to collaborate in this regard,” Kremlev wrote. 

The Russian oligarch is a close ally to Russian President Vladimir Putin and traveled with the head of state to China shortly before Trump Jr.’s wedding, according to reports from Chinese state media. In April, Putin presented Kremlev with the Order of Friendship, a high-level state honor. 

Additionally, the Ukrainian government has personally sanctioned Kremlev due to his close proximity to the Russian leader. 

Kremlev attended Trump Jr.’s 50-person wedding festivities with a group who spoke Russian and “whose presence puzzled other attendees,” ProPublica reported. 

How much did he pay and why?

Kremlev reportedly covered hundreds of thousands of dollars to fund the cost of Trump Jr.’s after-party events in the Bahamas. 

The Russian oligarch rented a private island that has a nightly price tag of $100,000 and a fireworks show from a company that charges around $70,000 per event, according to ProPublica. 

He made these payments through a Dubai-based entity affiliated with the IBA. 

A spokesperson for Trump Jr. did not deny the wedding payments in a statement to ProPublica, saying that Kremlev was “a personal friend” of the president’s eldest son. 

What are the Trumps saying?

Trump Jr. and his new wife, Bettina Trump, forcefully defended the gift in a statement shared on Instagram amid public criticism. 

“Our friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” the couple wrote in the post. “It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful.”

Trump did not attend the nuptials or after-party events, citing his executive responsibilities and the Iran war when asked by reporters about his plans ahead of the wedding. 

“While I very much wanted to be with my son, Don Jr., and the newest member of the Trump Family, his soon to be wife, Bettina, circumstances pertaining to Government, and my love for the United States of America, do not allow me to do so,” Trump wrote on Truth Social. 

In a statement shared by the White House with The New York Times on Monday, the president said he had “no idea” who Kremlev was and noted that the Russian oligarch “didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”

What are critics saying?

Democratic lawmakers were quick to condemn this unusual wedding gift from the Russian oligarch. 

In a speech from the Senate floor on Monday evening, Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) called it “naked corruption in plain view.”

“This was a Russian party organized and paid for by someone in Vladimir Putin’s inner circle,” Murphy said. “This has never happened before in the history of the United States of America. Never before has a foreign enemy of the United States paid for the family wedding of the president.”

Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Md.), the ranking member on the House Judiciary Committee, accused the Trump administration of “Putin-style corruption and authoritarianism” in a Monday social media post. 

“When Russian oligarchs pay for American oligarchs’ weddings, it’s a very sweet and romantic gesture, but we know who’s really getting married,” Raskin wrote. 

He added, “Let the oligarchs marry — the American people want a divorce of all of them.”

Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Calif.), a member of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, noted previous efforts from Russia to influence U.S. elections. 

“Now, we have more evidence that you’ve got a Russian oligarch paying money to a member of the Trump family,” he told MeidasTouch at the Capitol on Monday. “This is very, very scandalous, and we need an explanation from the president and his son.” 

Are there rules on these kinds of gifts?

Presidential families are typically expected under ethical norms to not accept expensive gifts from foreign adversaries to avoid the appearance of improper external influences. 

While Trump Jr. does not hold an official role in the Trump administration, he has been an influential member during his father’s presidency. In the last presidential election, he successfully advocated for his friend, now-Vice President JD Vance, to be selected as Trump’s running mate. 

Russia has a particularly thorny history with attempting to push its political agenda through U.S. officials. The Russian government and Putin have worked to interfere in both the 2016 and 2020 U.S. presidential elections, according to U.S. national security reports. 

This gift also came amid the Trump administration’s precarious efforts to broker a peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine to end the yearslong conflict. Earlier this month, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to both countries to meet with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.

data.title: Armenia is turning westward — the West should take it seriously
data.description:
Something remarkable is happening in Armenia. For decades one of Russia’s closest allies in the former Soviet Union, the country is preparing to apply for membership in the European Union. 

Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told parliament last month that Armenia intends to submit a formal application “in the near future,” and Moscow’s reaction has already demonstrated how consequential the choice could be.

Armenia will need help. 

Russia and its partners in the Eurasian Economic Union have been pressing Armenia to choose between the two blocs. Moscow has warned of economic consequences. Restrictions on Armenian exports to Russia have already become a source of grievance for Armenian farmers.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded to Pashinyan’s announcement by warning of “deep trade contradictions that will primarily harm Armenia.” The message is unmistakably clear: Russia has considerable power to make Armenia’s journey to Europe painful. 

There is another risk. Armenia could incur the costs of leaving the Russian orbit without ever being securely anchored in the West. It is an old problem for the world’s oldest Christian nation. Armenia has spent much of its history maneuvering between greater powers in search of security, from Rome and Persia to Russia and the West.

Eventually, Russia inherited that role, emerging as the Christian great power capable of challenging Persian and Ottoman domination. That security logic endured into the post-Soviet era. After 1991, Armenia faced Azerbaijan, a closed border with Turkey and no comparable Western security guarantee. In that context, it accepted strategic dependence on Moscow in return for protection.

But then the bargain broke down. The 2020 war with Azerbaijan badly damaged Armenian confidence in Russia. The crises that followed deepened the rupture, culminating in Azerbaijan’s 2023 takeover of Nagorno-Karabakh and the flight of virtually its entire ethnic Armenian population. Russia remained Armenia’s formal ally, but Armenians increasingly concluded that the alliance had failed to provide the protection for which they had sacrificed so much strategic freedom.

It would be easy to interpret what followed as Armenia simply searching for a new protector. But previous geopolitical turns were largely exercises in survival. Today, the shift runs deeper. The West is increasingly where Armenians themselves see their country’s future. Armenia’s technology sector is integrated into global markets. Younger Armenians increasingly look to Europe and the United States for professional, educational and cultural opportunities.

Then there is the diaspora. The U.S. is home to the world’s largest Armenian community outside the former Soviet Union. A deeper U.S.-Armenian relationship could turn that community from an advocate into a conduit for capital, expertise, technology and institutional connections.

That is why Pashinyan’s EU announcement is not simply a European story. Armenia’s movement toward Europe is occurring alongside a potentially transformative relationship with the U.S., most visibly through the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity, or TRIPP.

That U.S.-brokered project envisions a 43-kilometer transit route across southern Armenia connecting Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan and Turkey. It could eventually link Central Asia with Europe while reducing regional dependence on Russia and Iran, while creating opportunities for U.S.-Armenian cooperation in infrastructure, technology, energy and trade. 

After a major agreement was reached in June, last month Pashinyan met senior U.S. officials specifically to advance the project, with both sides promising more visible practical steps soon. Negotiations to establish the joint U.S.-Armenian development company are also nearing completion, creating the prospect of sustained American involvement in Armenia’s infrastructure, technology and trade. 

TRIPP and EU accession are therefore parts of the same geopolitical story. Europe offers Armenia an institutional destination. The U.S. can offer strategic connectivity, technology and investment, reinforced by an Armenian American community uniquely capable of knitting the two countries together.

If those relationships deepen, Armenia’s Western orientation would cease to depend on the preference of one government or prime minister. It would become rooted in where Armenian companies do business, where investment comes from and how the country connects to the world. 

This does not mean Armenia is simply exchanging Moscow for Washington. It wants consequential relationships with Europe and the U.S., but also with China, India, Iran and others.  

For a country whose history has repeatedly left it dependent on a single external protector, diversification is itself a form of sovereignty. EU membership, however, would be different in kind. It would eventually place Armenia inside a Western political, economic and institutional system. Combined with an expanding American relationship, it would amount to a genuine geopolitical realignment.

Armenia has attempted a Western turn during a period of Russian weakness before. When the Russian Empire collapsed in 1917, independent Armenia similarly looked West. Woodrow Wilson became the symbol of Armenian hopes for an external guarantee, but Western sympathy never became enforceable protection. In the aftermath of the Armenian Genocide, caught between Turkish forces and Bolshevik Russia, the First Republic disappeared in 1920.

A century later, Armenians are taking another chance. The West has an opportunity to do it right this time.

Grigor Hovhannissian is a former Armenian ambassador to the United States and Mexico and a former deputy foreign minister of Armenia.

data.title: California Democrat: 'We need to have a safety stand-down with AI'
data.description:
Rep. George Whitesides (D-Calif.) on Monday said that the U.S. needs “a safety stand-down” regarding AI amid growing calls for regulation coming from both the tech industry and members of Congress.

“I’m setting out a vision for how we need to develop AI,” Whitesides told NewsNation’s Blake Burman on “The Hill.” “I think we need, from my experience in the aerospace industry, working on accident recoveries and accident processes, that we need to have a safety stand-down with AI for at least one month for all the companies. Just one month.”

Asked by Burman about what he meant by a “safety stand-down,” Whitesides replied that consumers’ everyday AI usage would continue but that the “research on the frontier models, pushing forward that frontier, which is what people are scared about, would pause for a month while we do one thing.”

“We get the companies in the room, and we get experts, independent experts in the government, to talk about what are the red lines, what are the lines in the sand that we will not go past,” he continued. “We do not have that today. We need to have a common vision. And then Congress needs to work with those companies to put those red lines and lines in the sand into law.”

The California Democrat lambasted the fact that House members will leave Washington this week for a seven-week recess, suggesting that the “American people are scared.”

“They do not understand what’s happening in AI,” he continued. “And the leaders of these companies are saying actively, as your piece led in, that they want to slow down too. In fact, they want to have regulation. And so I think we need to stay in D.C. to work on this. And it’s crucial if we’re going to get real work done on this issue.”

Whitesides was previously NASA’s chief of staff and the former CEO of Virgin Galactic. His district covers much of northern Los Angeles County, including the cities of Santa Clarita, Palmdale and Lancaster, and the unincorporated areas of Stevenson Ranch and Castaic.

Republican leaders and President Trump have thrown cold water on integrating any federal safeguards on AI.

Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) dismissed the idea this week, while Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) said Monday that any regulation should be done in a “light-touch way that doesn’t squash innovation.”

Trump wrote on Truth Social that the only guardrails needed for AI “is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!” He wrote in a separate post that fears that AI could destroy humanity is a “hoax.”

This grave concern over AI made headlines last week after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon wrote on social media that those who develop AI ” earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade.” Fellow Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger echoed this, saying, “we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans.”

Over the weekend, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said that artificial intelligence development must slow down to inlclude more safeguards, a call that was later backed by Sam Altman and Elon Musk.
